title: How Bacteria Take a Vote
body:
Bacteria were long regarded as the most solitary of organisms. A single cell divides, the two daughter cells drift apart, and whatever either of them accomplishes it appears to accomplish alone. This assumption began to erode in the 1970s, when microbiologists turned their attention to an unremarkable marine bacterium called Vibrio fischeri. The organism is luminescent, and it lives in the light organs of certain squid, which use the glow to erase their silhouettes against moonlit water. What puzzled researchers was not the light itself but its timing. A flask of these bacteria grown in the laboratory remained dark for hours and then, quite abruptly, began to shine.

The explanation could not be that individual cells were switching on at random, for that would have produced a gradual brightening rather than a sudden one. Nor could the cells be reacting to some change in the flask itself, since the medium was deliberately held constant. The clue lay in density. Light appeared only once the population had grown past a certain size. Something, it seemed, allowed each bacterium to register how many others surrounded it, and only when that number was sufficient did the cells commit to the considerable expense of producing light. The bacteria, in other words, were behaving less like a crowd of individuals than like a single body awaiting a cue.

That something proved to be a small molecule. Each cell continuously releases a chemical signal, later named an autoinducer, into its surroundings, and each cell also carries a receptor for it. When the population is sparse, the molecule diffuses away and its concentration remains negligible. As the cells multiply, however, the signal accumulates faster than it disperses, until it crosses a threshold at which the receptors are occupied and a whole battery of genes is switched on at once. The process is now called quorum sensing, a term borrowed from parliamentary procedure: nothing is decided until enough members are present to act.

The discovery would have remained a curiosity of marine biology had the same mechanism not turned out to be nearly universal. Many pathogens, it emerged, use quorum sensing to schedule their assault on a host. Releasing toxins while still few in number would merely alert the immune system to a threat it could easily eliminate; by staying silent until their numbers are overwhelming, the invaders improve their odds considerably. This insight has suggested an unfamiliar strategy for medicine. Rather than killing bacteria outright, the approach that has driven the rise of resistance, one might instead jam their communication, leaving the cells alive but unable to coordinate. A drug that merely silences an organism exerts less pressure to evolve around it than one that threatens the organism with death. Whether that difference is large enough to matter remains an open question.

questions.question: According to paragraph 1, what benefit do certain squid gain from luminescent bacteria?

choices.A: The bacteria illuminate prey that the squid would otherwise be unable to see
choices.B: The glow conceals the outline the squid would otherwise cast in lit water
choices.C: The bacteria warn the squid of predators approaching from below
choices.D: The light attracts other members of the squid's own species

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says "it lives in the light organs of certain squid, which use the glow to erase their silhouettes against moonlit water", so the light is used to hide the squid's outline. The functions in A, C and D (finding prey, warning of predators, attracting other squid) are not described anywhere in the passage.

questions.question: Why does the author mention that "the medium was deliberately held constant"?

choices.A: To show that the experiment was difficult to carry out
choices.B: To explain why the bacteria grew more slowly than expected
choices.C: To introduce the chemical signal described in the next paragraph
choices.D: To eliminate a competing explanation for the sudden appearance of light

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 first rejects the idea with "could not be that individual cells were switching on at random", and then says "Nor could the cells be reacting to some change in the flask itself, since the medium was deliberately held constant". The mention of the constant medium is there to rule out a competing hypothesis, a change in the environment; after this process of elimination the paragraph moves on to density.

questions.question: The word "negligible" in paragraph 3 is closest in meaning to
questions.explanation: In the context of "When the population is sparse, the molecule diffuses away and its concentration remains negligible", the word means that diffusion keeps the concentration at a level too low to have any effect. B, 'impossible to measure', goes too far, and the context does not support C or D.

questions.question: The word "it" in the phrase "each cell also carries a receptor for it" refers to
questions.explanation: In "Each cell continuously releases a chemical signal, later named an autoinducer, into its surroundings, and each cell also carries a receptor for it", what the receptor binds is the chemical signal (the autoinducer) that has been released. A reading in which the receptor receives itself or the cell does not make sense.

questions.question: What does the author suggest about drugs that block bacterial communication?

choices.A: They are already more widely used than conventional antibiotics
choices.B: They may provoke resistance less strongly, though this is not yet settled
choices.C: They work only against pathogens that produce visible light
choices.D: They eliminate bacteria faster than drugs that kill cells directly

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says "A drug that merely silences an organism exerts less pressure to evolve around it than one that threatens the organism with death", but immediately qualifies this with "Whether that difference is large enough to matter remains an open question". B reflects both of these points. A's claim about how widely the drugs are used is not in the passage. C confuses light production with the ability to cause disease, and D contradicts "leaving the cells alive".

abruptly.etymology: Latin ab- 'away' + rumpere 'to break' → 'as if broken off'
abruptly.usage_in_passage: The word abruptly in "then, quite abruptly, began to shine" is the central puzzle of the passage itself, and its contrast with "gradual brightening" in paragraph 2 drives the argument.
abruptly.context_sentence: A flask of these bacteria grown in the laboratory remained dark for hours and then, quite abruptly, began to shine.

accomplish.etymology: Latin ad- 'to' + complere 'to fill' → 'to carry through'
accomplish.definition: To succeed in doing something; to achieve.
accomplish.usage_in_passage: It is repeated in the same sentence as a pair with accomplishes, and is placed where it puts the stress on "alone".
accomplish.context_sentence: A single cell divides, the two daughter cells drift apart, and whatever either of them accomplishes it appears to accomplish alone.

accomplishes.etymology: Latin ad- 'to' + complere 'to fill' → 'to carry through'
accomplishes.usage_in_passage: In "whatever either of them accomplishes it appears to accomplish alone", it states openly the premise that the unit of action is the individual cell.
accomplishes.context_sentence: A single cell divides, the two daughter cells drift apart, and whatever either of them accomplishes it appears to accomplish alone.

accumulates.etymology: Latin ad- 'to' + cumulus 'a heap' → 'to pile up'
accumulates.usage_in_passage: "the signal accumulates faster than it disperses" explains the threshold as a competition between two rates, accumulation and diffusion.
accumulates.context_sentence: As the cells multiply, however, the signal accumulates faster than it disperses, until it crosses a threshold at which the receptors are occupied and a whole battery of genes is switched on at once.

alive.etymology: Old English on life 'in a state of life'
alive.usage_in_passage: "leaving the cells alive but unable to coordinate" is the key point of the new strategy; the fact that the cells are not killed is the premise of the argument about pressure toward resistance.
alive.context_sentence: Rather than killing bacteria outright, the approach that has driven the rise of resistance, one might instead jam their communication, leaving the cells alive but unable to coordinate.

apart.usage_in_passage: In "drift apart" it shows that the cells produced by division no longer have anything to do with each other, which stands in direct opposition to the later "like a single body".
apart.context_sentence: A single cell divides, the two daughter cells drift apart, and whatever either of them accomplishes it appears to accomplish alone.

assault.etymology: Latin ad- 'to' + saltare 'to leap' → 'to leap upon'
assault.usage_in_passage: "schedule their assault on a host" presents infection as a planned attack and shows that the issue is one of timing.
assault.context_sentence: Many pathogens, it emerged, use quorum sensing to schedule their assault on a host.

assumption.etymology: Latin ad- 'to' + sumere 'to take' → 'to take in as a premise'
assumption.definition: Something accepted as true without proof; a premise.
assumption.usage_in_passage: "This assumption began to erode" is the turning point of the paragraph. Looking back, it redefines everything said up to that point as an assumption, not a fact.
assumption.context_sentence: This assumption began to erode in the 1970s, when microbiologists turned their attention to an unremarkable marine bacterium called Vibrio fischeri.

autoinducer.etymology: Greek auto- 'self' + Latin inducere 'to lead in' + -er
autoinducer.definition: A signal molecule that induces the expression of the genes of the cells that produce it.
autoinducer.usage_in_passage: By inserting "later named an autoinducer", which notes that the name was given afterwards, the passage keeps the order in which the discovery moved from observing the phenomenon to identifying the mechanism.
autoinducer.context_sentence: Each cell continuously releases a chemical signal, later named an autoinducer, into its surroundings, and each cell also carries a receptor for it.

awaiting.definition: Waiting for something that is expected.
awaiting.usage_in_passage: "like a single body awaiting a cue" presents the group of cells as a single agent waiting for a signal, and is a figurative preview of quorum sensing.
awaiting.context_sentence: The bacteria, in other words, were behaving less like a crowd of individuals than like a single body awaiting a cue.

bacteria.etymology: Plural of Greek bakterion 'small staff' → rod-shaped microorganisms
bacteria.usage_in_passage: In the opening "Bacteria were long regarded as the most solitary of organisms", it is the subject of the accepted view that the passage sets out to overturn.
bacteria.context_sentence: Bacteria were long regarded as the most solitary of organisms.

bacterium.usage_in_passage: "an unremarkable marine bacterium called Vibrio fischeri" uses the singular and narrows the discussion to one concrete species.
bacterium.context_sentence: This assumption began to erode in the 1970s, when microbiologists turned their attention to an unremarkable marine bacterium called Vibrio fischeri.

behaving.usage_in_passage: "were behaving less like a crowd of individuals than like a single body" explicitly denies the word solitary from paragraph 1.
behaving.context_sentence: The bacteria, in other words, were behaving less like a crowd of individuals than like a single body awaiting a cue.

biology.definition: The scientific study of living things.
biology.usage_in_passage: "a curiosity of marine biology" shows that the discovery was at first confined to a single field.
biology.context_sentence: The discovery would have remained a curiosity of marine biology had the same mechanism not turned out to be nearly universal.

borrowed.etymology: Old English borgian 'to take a pledge' → 'to borrow'
borrowed.definition: Taken from another source and used as one's own.
borrowed.usage_in_passage: "a term borrowed from parliamentary procedure" states openly that the biological term came from the vocabulary of a human institution.
borrowed.context_sentence: The process is now called quorum sensing, a term borrowed from parliamentary procedure: nothing is decided until enough members are present to act.

brightening.usage_in_passage: "a gradual brightening" turns into a noun the contrasting phenomenon that did not in fact occur, and presents it as a counterfactual.
brightening.context_sentence: The explanation could not be that individual cells were switching on at random, for that would have produced a gradual brightening rather than a sudden one.

carries.etymology: Latin carrus 'wagon' → 'to transport, to be equipped with'
carries.definition: Has or possesses as a part of itself.
carries.usage_in_passage: The word also in "each cell also carries a receptor for it" shows that the same cell does both the sending and the receiving.
carries.context_sentence: Each cell continuously releases a chemical signal, later named an autoinducer, into its surroundings, and each cell also carries a receptor for it.

clue.etymology: Middle English clewe 'ball of thread', from the thread used to find the way out of the labyrinth
clue.definition: A piece of evidence that helps to solve a problem.
clue.usage_in_passage: "The clue lay in density" is the hinge sentence that turns from the process of elimination to a positive hypothesis.

commit.definition: To devote resources to a course of action; to go ahead with it.
commit.usage_in_passage: "did the cells commit to the considerable expense of producing light" presents light production as an investment that has a cost, and explains why the cells need to count their numbers.
commit.context_sentence: Something, it seemed, allowed each bacterium to register how many others surrounded it, and only when that number was sufficient did the cells commit to the considerable expense of producing light.

concentration.etymology: con- 'together' + Latin centrum 'centre' → 'a gathering at the centre'
concentration.definition: The amount of a substance present in a given volume.
concentration.usage_in_passage: "its concentration remains negligible" translates the number of cells, a quantity the cells cannot count, into concentration, a quantity that can be measured. This substitution is the key to the whole mechanism.
concentration.context_sentence: When the population is sparse, the molecule diffuses away and its concentration remains negligible.

considerable.definition: Fairly large in amount or degree.
considerable.usage_in_passage: "the considerable expense" shows how large the cost of producing light is, and supports the logic of making it depend on density.
considerable.context_sentence: Something, it seemed, allowed each bacterium to register how many others surrounded it, and only when that number was sufficient did the cells commit to the considerable expense of producing light.

considerably.etymology: con- + Latin sidus 'star' → 'to a degree worth careful thought' → 'substantially'
considerably.definition: To a fairly large degree; much.
considerably.usage_in_passage: "improve their odds considerably" asserts how large the effect is, and supports the reason why this strategy is so widespread.
considerably.context_sentence: by staying silent until their numbers are overwhelming, the invaders improve their odds considerably.

constant.usage_in_passage: "held constant" is a set phrase of experimental science for a controlled condition, and it is the basis for Question 2.
constant.context_sentence: Nor could the cells be reacting to some change in the flask itself, since the medium was deliberately held constant.

continuously.etymology: Latin con- 'together' + tenere 'to hold' → 'without a break'
continuously.usage_in_passage: The word continuously in "Each cell continuously releases a chemical signal" shows that the release is not conditional but goes on all the time. This is the premise that makes concentration an indicator of number.
continuously.context_sentence: Each cell continuously releases a chemical signal, later named an autoinducer, into its surroundings, and each cell also carries a receptor for it.

coordinate.etymology: Latin co- 'together' + ordinare 'to put in order'
coordinate.definition: To act together in an organized way.
coordinate.usage_in_passage: "unable to coordinate" shows that the target is the collective behaviour itself, which the passage has described throughout.
coordinate.context_sentence: Rather than killing bacteria outright, the approach that has driven the rise of resistance, one might instead jam their communication, leaving the cells alive but unable to coordinate.

crowd.definition: A large group gathered together without organization.
crowd.usage_in_passage: "less like a crowd of individuals" refers to a collection that is merely large in number, and is set against the organized single body.
crowd.context_sentence: The bacteria, in other words, were behaving less like a crowd of individuals than like a single body awaiting a cue.

curiosity.definition: An unusual thing that is interesting mainly to specialists.
curiosity.usage_in_passage: "would have remained a curiosity of marine biology" shows where the discovery stood before its universality became clear, and creates a gap with what follows.
curiosity.context_sentence: The discovery would have remained a curiosity of marine biology had the same mechanism not turned out to be nearly universal.

deliberately.etymology: Latin de- 'completely' + librare 'to weigh' → 'after careful weighing'
deliberately.usage_in_passage: The word deliberately in "the medium was deliberately held constant" shows that the constant condition was not an accident but part of the experimental design, and this justifies ruling out the competing hypothesis.
deliberately.context_sentence: Nor could the cells be reacting to some change in the flask itself, since the medium was deliberately held constant.

density.definition: The number of individuals in a given space.
density.usage_in_passage: "The clue lay in density" introduces the key concept of the passage. Everything said about quorum sensing afterwards is developed as an explanation of this dependence on density.

diffuses.etymology: Latin dis- 'in all directions' + fundere 'to pour' → 'to spread out'
diffuses.definition: Spreads out through the surrounding space.
diffuses.usage_in_passage: "the molecule diffuses away" gives the reason why, at low density, the signal is diluted and does not reach the cells.
diffuses.context_sentence: When the population is sparse, the molecule diffuses away and its concentration remains negligible.

discovery.etymology: dis- (negation) + Latin cooperire 'to cover' → 'to take the cover off'
discovery.definition: The act of finding something that was not known before.
discovery.usage_in_passage: "The discovery would have remained a curiosity" opens with a hypothetical past form and prepares the reversal: in fact this did not happen.
discovery.context_sentence: The discovery would have remained a curiosity of marine biology had the same mechanism not turned out to be nearly universal.

disperses.etymology: Latin dis- 'in all directions' + spargere 'to scatter' → 'to scatter'
disperses.usage_in_passage: "faster than it disperses" is the counterpart of accumulates, and implies that the point where this balance is reversed is the threshold.
disperses.context_sentence: As the cells multiply, however, the signal accumulates faster than it disperses, until it crosses a threshold at which the receptors are occupied and a whole battery of genes is switched on at once.

divides.usage_in_passage: "A single cell divides" describes bacterial growth in its smallest unit and, paired with the following drift apart, gives a picture of the accepted view that bacteria 'multiply but do not connect'.
divides.context_sentence: A single cell divides, the two daughter cells drift apart, and whatever either of them accomplishes it appears to accomplish alone.

drift.etymology: From Old English drifan 'to drive' → 'to be carried along'
drift.definition: To be carried slowly away, as if by a current.
drift.usage_in_passage: "the two daughter cells drift apart" expresses the assumption that the relationship between the cells is cut off after division.
drift.context_sentence: A single cell divides, the two daughter cells drift apart, and whatever either of them accomplishes it appears to accomplish alone.

driven.etymology: Past participle of Old English drifan 'to drive'
driven.usage_in_passage: "the approach that has driven the rise of resistance" names the conventional method as the cause of the spread of resistance, and gives the grounds for needing an alternative.
driven.context_sentence: Rather than killing bacteria outright, the approach that has driven the rise of resistance, one might instead jam their communication, leaving the cells alive but unable to coordinate.

eliminate.etymology: Latin e- 'out' + limen 'threshold' → 'to put out over the threshold'
eliminate.usage_in_passage: "a threat it could easily eliminate" sets up the premise that the bacteria are wiped out while they are few, and supports the logic of the strategy of silence.
eliminate.context_sentence: Releasing toxins while still few in number would merely alert the immune system to a threat it could easily eliminate;

emerged.etymology: Latin e- 'out' + mergere 'to dip' → 'to rise to the surface'
emerged.usage_in_passage: The inserted phrase "it emerged" moves the sentence forward while keeping the order in time: this was found out later.
emerged.context_sentence: Many pathogens, it emerged, use quorum sensing to schedule their assault on a host.

erase.etymology: Latin e- 'out' + radere 'to scrape' → 'to scrape away'
erase.definition: To remove completely; to wipe out.
erase.usage_in_passage: "erase their silhouettes against moonlit water" is the opposite of 'illuminate', and expresses in one word the paradox of using light as a tool for concealment.
erase.context_sentence: The organism is luminescent, and it lives in the light organs of certain squid, which use the glow to erase their silhouettes against moonlit water.

erode.etymology: Latin e- 'out' + rodere 'to gnaw' → 'to wear away little by little'
erode.definition: To wear away or weaken gradually.
erode.usage_in_passage: "began to erode" is a word chosen for a gradual collapse, not a sudden rejection, and it suggests the build-up of research from the 1970s onward.
erode.context_sentence: This assumption began to erode in the 1970s, when microbiologists turned their attention to an unremarkable marine bacterium called Vibrio fischeri.

evolve.usage_in_passage: "less pressure to evolve around it" formulates the gaining of resistance as a question of evolution.
evolve.context_sentence: A drug that merely silences an organism exerts less pressure to evolve around it than one that threatens the organism with death.

exerts.etymology: Latin ex- 'out' + serere 'to join' → 'to apply force'
exerts.usage_in_passage: "exerts less pressure to evolve around it" introduces the viewpoint of stronger or weaker evolutionary selection pressure, and states the theoretical advantage of the new strategy.
exerts.context_sentence: A drug that merely silences an organism exerts less pressure to evolve around it than one that threatens the organism with death.

expense.etymology: Latin ex- 'out' + pendere 'to weigh, to pay'
expense.usage_in_passage: "the considerable expense of producing light" introduces an economic metaphor that treats light production as a biochemical expenditure.
expense.context_sentence: Something, it seemed, allowed each bacterium to register how many others surrounded it, and only when that number was sufficient did the cells commit to the considerable expense of producing light.

explanation.etymology: Latin ex- 'out' + planare 'to make flat' → 'to smooth out, to unravel'
explanation.definition: A statement that makes clear why something happens.
explanation.usage_in_passage: "The explanation could not be that" is the starting point of the process of elimination, and announces a structure in which the candidate hypotheses are rejected one by one over the next two sentences.
explanation.context_sentence: The explanation could not be that individual cells were switching on at random, for that would have produced a gradual brightening rather than a sudden one.

flask.definition: A glass container used in laboratory experiments.
flask.usage_in_passage: "A flask of these bacteria grown in the laboratory" moves the place of observation from the wild to the laboratory, and makes possible the discussion of controlled conditions in paragraph 2.
flask.context_sentence: A flask of these bacteria grown in the laboratory remained dark for hours and then, quite abruptly, began to shine.

glow.usage_in_passage: In "use the glow to erase their silhouettes", it shows that the light works as a means to an end.
glow.context_sentence: The organism is luminescent, and it lives in the light organs of certain squid, which use the glow to erase their silhouettes against moonlit water.

gradual.usage_in_passage: "would have produced a gradual brightening rather than a sudden one" states the result that the random-switching hypothesis predicts, and rejects it because it does not match the observation.
gradual.context_sentence: The explanation could not be that individual cells were switching on at random, for that would have produced a gradual brightening rather than a sudden one.

grown.etymology: Past participle of Old English growan 'to grow'
grown.usage_in_passage: "grown in the laboratory" points to artificial culture conditions and makes clear that the observation is separate from the symbiosis found in nature.
grown.context_sentence: A flask of these bacteria grown in the laboratory remained dark for hours and then, quite abruptly, began to shine.

immune.etymology: Latin im- (negation) + munus 'duty' → 'exempt from duty' → 'relating to immunity'
immune.definition: Relating to the body's defences against infection.
immune.usage_in_passage: "alert the immune system to a threat" introduces the host's power to fight back against the pathogens' calculation.
immune.context_sentence: Releasing toxins while still few in number would merely alert the immune system to a threat it could easily eliminate;

insight.definition: A clear understanding of how something works.
insight.usage_in_passage: "This insight has suggested an unfamiliar strategy for medicine" is the sentence that bridges a finding of basic research to its application.
insight.context_sentence: This insight has suggested an unfamiliar strategy for medicine.

invaders.definition: Those that enter by force in order to attack.
invaders.usage_in_passage: "the invaders improve their odds considerably" presents the pathogens as a military force and keeps the metaphor of assault consistent.
invaders.context_sentence: by staying silent until their numbers are overwhelming, the invaders improve their odds considerably.

killing.usage_in_passage: "Rather than killing bacteria outright" sums up in one word the principle of conventional antibiotics, and is the starting point for the alternative.
killing.context_sentence: Rather than killing bacteria outright, the approach that has driven the rise of resistance, one might instead jam their communication, leaving the cells alive but unable to coordinate.

luminescent.usage_in_passage: "The organism is luminescent" introduces the very thing the passage observes. It refers to biological light production, in contrast to incandescent, which involves heat.
luminescent.context_sentence: The organism is luminescent, and it lives in the light organs of certain squid, which use the glow to erase their silhouettes against moonlit water.

mechanism.definition: The way in which a process works.
mechanism.usage_in_passage: "had the same mechanism not turned out to be nearly universal" ties together the squid's light and the pathogens' release of toxins as one and the same process.
mechanism.context_sentence: The discovery would have remained a curiosity of marine biology had the same mechanism not turned out to be nearly universal.

merely.usage_in_passage: The word merely in "would merely alert the immune system" dismisses in one word the effect of an early release: it would only be a warning and bring no benefit.
merely.context_sentence: Releasing toxins while still few in number would merely alert the immune system to a threat it could easily eliminate;

microbiologists.usage_in_passage: "when microbiologists turned their attention to" identifies who it was that undermined the accepted view.
microbiologists.context_sentence: This assumption began to erode in the 1970s, when microbiologists turned their attention to an unremarkable marine bacterium called Vibrio fischeri.

molecule.definition: The smallest unit of a chemical substance.
molecule.usage_in_passage: "a small molecule" brings the abstract ability to sense density down to a physical mechanism.
molecule.context_sentence: That something proved to be a small molecule.

moonlit.etymology: moon 'moon' + lit (past participle of light) → 'lit by the moon'
moonlit.definition: Lit by the light of the moon.
moonlit.usage_in_passage: "against moonlit water" identifies the light source that produces the outline, and makes it clear why giving off light works as concealment.
moonlit.context_sentence: The organism is luminescent, and it lives in the light organs of certain squid, which use the glow to erase their silhouettes against moonlit water.

multiply.etymology: Latin multus 'many' + plicare 'to fold' → 'to become many times more'
multiply.definition: To increase in number by reproducing.
multiply.usage_in_passage: The word however in "As the cells multiply, however" marks the turn to the high-density side.
multiply.context_sentence: As the cells multiply, however, the signal accumulates faster than it disperses, until it crosses a threshold at which the receptors are occupied and a whole battery of genes is switched on at once.

negligible.etymology: Latin neglegere 'to disregard' + -ible → 'that may be disregarded'
negligible.definition: So small that it can be ignored.
negligible.usage_in_passage: "its concentration remains negligible" means that the concentration is not zero but stays at a level that has no effect, and it is the basis for the answer to Question 3.
negligible.context_sentence: When the population is sparse, the molecule diffuses away and its concentration remains negligible.

occupied.etymology: Latin ob- 'toward' + capere 'to take' → 'to take up'
occupied.usage_in_passage: "the receptors are occupied" refers to the state in which the receptors are filled with the signal, which is the trigger for gene expression.
occupied.context_sentence: As the cells multiply, however, the signal accumulates faster than it disperses, until it crosses a threshold at which the receptors are occupied and a whole battery of genes is switched on at once.

odds.etymology: Old Norse oddi 'odd number, unevenness' → 'difference, chances'
odds.usage_in_passage: "improve their odds considerably" expresses the gain from the strategy of silence in the language of probability.
odds.context_sentence: by staying silent until their numbers are overwhelming, the invaders improve their odds considerably.

organism.usage_in_passage: In "The organism is luminescent" it rephrases bacterium from the previous sentence, keeping the same referent while avoiding repetition.
organism.context_sentence: Bacteria were long regarded as the most solitary of organisms.

organisms.etymology: Greek organon 'tool, organ' + -ism → 'something that has organs'
organisms.usage_in_passage: "the most solitary of organisms" places bacteria among living things in general and so stresses how exceptional they were thought to be.
organisms.context_sentence: Bacteria were long regarded as the most solitary of organisms.

organs.definition: Parts of the body that have a particular function.
organs.usage_in_passage: "the light organs of certain squid" shows at an early stage that the bacteria do not live alone but in a relationship with a host.
organs.context_sentence: The organism is luminescent, and it lives in the light organs of certain squid, which use the glow to erase their silhouettes against moonlit water.

outright.usage_in_passage: The word outright in "killing bacteria outright" shows how thorough the killing is, and stands in sharp opposition to the later "leaving the cells alive".
outright.context_sentence: Rather than killing bacteria outright, the approach that has driven the rise of resistance, one might instead jam their communication, leaving the cells alive but unable to coordinate.

overwhelming.etymology: over- 'over' + Middle English whelmen 'to turn upside down'
overwhelming.definition: Too great in number to be resisted.
overwhelming.usage_in_passage: "until their numbers are overwhelming" restates the threshold from the host's point of view, and corresponds to threshold in paragraph 3.
overwhelming.context_sentence: by staying silent until their numbers are overwhelming, the invaders improve their odds considerably.

parliamentary.usage_in_passage: "borrowed from parliamentary procedure: nothing is decided until enough members are present to act" explains the quorum metaphor explicitly, and connects the technical term to an institution the reader already knows.
parliamentary.context_sentence: The process is now called quorum sensing, a term borrowed from parliamentary procedure: nothing is decided until enough members are present to act.

pathogens.usage_in_passage: "Many pathogens, it emerged, use quorum sensing" is the turning point where the topic moves from marine life to medicine.
pathogens.context_sentence: Many pathogens, it emerged, use quorum sensing to schedule their assault on a host.

proved.usage_in_passage: "That something proved to be a small molecule" gives an answer to the unidentified "Something" at the end of paragraph 2 and links the two paragraphs.
proved.context_sentence: That something proved to be a small molecule.

puzzled.etymology: Origin unknown; from 16th-century English puzzle 'to bewilder'
puzzled.definition: Confused; caused someone to be unable to understand.
puzzled.usage_in_passage: "What puzzled researchers was not the light itself but its timing" is the turning sentence that moves the focus of the paragraph from whether there is light to when the light appears.
puzzled.context_sentence: What puzzled researchers was not the light itself but its timing.

quorum.etymology: Latin quorum, genitive plural of qui 'who'; from the wording used to state the minimum number of members for a meeting
quorum.definition: The minimum number of members that must be present for a group to make a decision.
quorum.usage_in_passage: "The process is now called quorum sensing" introduces the core term of the passage, and its meaning is then opened up immediately by the parliamentary metaphor.
quorum.context_sentence: The process is now called quorum sensing, a term borrowed from parliamentary procedure: nothing is decided until enough members are present to act.

reacting.usage_in_passage: "Nor could the cells be reacting to some change in the flask itself" presents the second candidate hypothesis (a reaction to the external environment) and rejects it straight away.
reacting.context_sentence: Nor could the cells be reacting to some change in the flask itself, since the medium was deliberately held constant.

receptor.definition: A molecule on a cell that binds a specific signal.
receptor.usage_in_passage: "a receptor for it" is the mechanism on the side that reads the signal, and it is also the sentence whose referent Question 4 asks about.
receptor.context_sentence: Each cell continuously releases a chemical signal, later named an autoinducer, into its surroundings, and each cell also carries a receptor for it.

receptors.definition: Molecules on a cell that bind a specific signal (plural form).
receptors.usage_in_passage: "the receptors are occupied" gives the molecular reality of reaching the threshold.
receptors.context_sentence: As the cells multiply, however, the signal accumulates faster than it disperses, until it crosses a threshold at which the receptors are occupied and a whole battery of genes is switched on at once.

regarded.etymology: re- 'again' + Latin gardare 'to look' → 'to look at repeatedly, to consider'
regarded.definition: Considered or thought of in a particular way.
regarded.usage_in_passage: The passive "were long regarded as" shows that this is not a fact but 'a view that was long believed', and it prepares for erode in the third sentence.
regarded.context_sentence: Bacteria were long regarded as the most solitary of organisms.

researchers.definition: People who carry out scientific investigation.
researchers.usage_in_passage: In "What puzzled researchers", it names who is asking the question and sets up the people who carry out the reasoning by elimination that follows.
researchers.context_sentence: What puzzled researchers was not the light itself but its timing.

resistance.definition: The ability of bacteria to survive a drug.
resistance.usage_in_passage: "the rise of resistance" introduces the real-world problem of drug resistance, and leads to the argument about evolution in the closing sentences.
resistance.context_sentence: Rather than killing bacteria outright, the approach that has driven the rise of resistance, one might instead jam their communication, leaving the cells alive but unable to coordinate.

shine.usage_in_passage: "began to shine" closes the paragraph and fixes the phenomenon that was observed.
shine.context_sentence: A flask of these bacteria grown in the laboratory remained dark for hours and then, quite abruptly, began to shine.

silences.etymology: Latin silere 'to be silent' + -ence → 'to make silent'
silences.usage_in_passage: "A drug that merely silences an organism" expresses in one word a mode of action that blocks communication without killing, and is the subject of the following exerts less pressure.
silences.context_sentence: A drug that merely silences an organism exerts less pressure to evolve around it than one that threatens the organism with death.

silent.definition: Showing no activity; making no signal.
silent.usage_in_passage: "by staying silent until their numbers are overwhelming" rephrases not releasing toxins as an active strategy.
silent.context_sentence: by staying silent until their numbers are overwhelming, the invaders improve their odds considerably.

silhouettes.etymology: From the name of Étienne de Silhouette, an 18th-century French finance minister
silhouettes.definition: Dark outlines seen against a lighter background.
silhouettes.usage_in_passage: "erase their silhouettes against moonlit water" gives the concrete scene of a shadow that stands out when seen from below.
silhouettes.context_sentence: The organism is luminescent, and it lives in the light organs of certain squid, which use the glow to erase their silhouettes against moonlit water.

solitary.usage_in_passage: "the most solitary of organisms" creates the opposition that runs through the whole passage. In the end this description is overturned by quorum sensing.
solitary.context_sentence: Bacteria were long regarded as the most solitary of organisms.

sparse.etymology: Latin sparsus, past participle of spargere 'to scatter' → 'thinly scattered'
sparse.definition: Thinly spread; few and far apart.
sparse.usage_in_passage: "When the population is sparse" sets the condition on the low-density side and, paired with the following multiply, describes both sides of the threshold.
sparse.context_sentence: When the population is sparse, the molecule diffuses away and its concentration remains negligible.

squid.etymology: Origin unknown; said to come from 17th-century sailors' slang
squid.definition: A soft-bodied sea animal with ten arms.
squid.usage_in_passage: "certain squid, which use the glow to erase their silhouettes" gives light production an ecological meaning, and is the basis for Question 1.
squid.context_sentence: The organism is luminescent, and it lives in the light organs of certain squid, which use the glow to erase their silhouettes against moonlit water.

sudden.usage_in_passage: The word one in "rather than a sudden one" stands for brightening, and it fixes in one word the nature of the light that was observed.
sudden.context_sentence: The explanation could not be that individual cells were switching on at random, for that would have produced a gradual brightening rather than a sudden one.

sufficient.etymology: Latin sub- 'from below' + facere 'to make' → 'to be enough'
sufficient.usage_in_passage: "only when that number was sufficient" announces in advance that a threshold exists, which is explained as a mechanism by threshold in paragraph 3.
sufficient.context_sentence: Something, it seemed, allowed each bacterium to register how many others surrounded it, and only when that number was sufficient did the cells commit to the considerable expense of producing light.

surrounded.etymology: Latin super- 'over' + undare 'to rise in waves' → 'to encircle'
surrounded.usage_in_passage: "register how many others surrounded it" puts into words for the first time the central claim of the passage, that each cell senses the number around it.
surrounded.context_sentence: Something, it seemed, allowed each bacterium to register how many others surrounded it, and only when that number was sufficient did the cells commit to the considerable expense of producing light.

surroundings.etymology: super- 'over' + undare 'to rise in waves' → 'what encircles'
surroundings.definition: The area and conditions around something.
surroundings.usage_in_passage: "into its surroundings" shows that the chemical signal goes out into the shared space outside the cell. This shared space is what makes it possible to total up the numbers.
surroundings.context_sentence: Each cell continuously releases a chemical signal, later named an autoinducer, into its surroundings, and each cell also carries a receptor for it.

threat.usage_in_passage: "a threat it could easily eliminate" places the pathogens, while they are few, as they are judged from the side of the immune system.
threat.context_sentence: Releasing toxins while still few in number would merely alert the immune system to a threat it could easily eliminate;

threatens.usage_in_passage: "one that threatens the organism with death" refers to conventional drugs and, through the contrast with silences, explains the difference in selection pressure. The reservation in the final sentence questions how large this difference is.
threatens.context_sentence: A drug that merely silences an organism exerts less pressure to evolve around it than one that threatens the organism with death.

threshold.definition: The level at which something starts to happen.
threshold.usage_in_passage: "until it crosses a threshold" is the word that explains abruptly from paragraph 1 in terms of mechanism. It refers to the point where continuous accumulation turns into a discontinuous response.
threshold.context_sentence: As the cells multiply, however, the signal accumulates faster than it disperses, until it crosses a threshold at which the receptors are occupied and a whole battery of genes is switched on at once.

toxins.definition: Poisonous substances produced by living things.
toxins.usage_in_passage: "Releasing toxins while still few in number" is the concrete subject of the argument about why an attack that comes too early is a disadvantage.
toxins.context_sentence: Releasing toxins while still few in number would merely alert the immune system to a threat it could easily eliminate;

unable.usage_in_passage: The word but in "alive but unable to coordinate" shows the aim of the new strategy, which separates survival from function.
unable.context_sentence: Rather than killing bacteria outright, the approach that has driven the rise of resistance, one might instead jam their communication, leaving the cells alive but unable to coordinate.

unfamiliar.definition: Not known before; new and different from the usual.
unfamiliar.usage_in_passage: "an unfamiliar strategy for medicine" announces the contrast with the conventional method that the next sentence presents with its Rather than construction.
unfamiliar.context_sentence: This insight has suggested an unfamiliar strategy for medicine.

unremarkable.definition: Not special in any way; ordinary.
unremarkable.usage_in_passage: The modest introduction "an unremarkable marine bacterium" makes the later contrast with "nearly universal" stand out.
unremarkable.context_sentence: This assumption began to erode in the 1970s, when microbiologists turned their attention to an unremarkable marine bacterium called Vibrio fischeri.
